concepts.name: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
concepts.description: Every mass attracts every other mass with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres: F = G·M·m/r². The constant G = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ m³/(kg·s²). Questions compute the gravitational force between a central body and an orbiting body and explain how a change in distance (halving r) quadruples the force.
core_skills: State and apply F = G·M·m/r² to compute gravitational force magnitude
Explain the inverse-square dependence: doubling distance quarters the force, halving distance quadruples it
Use G = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ m³/(kg·s²) with consistent SI units
Distinguish the force on the orbiting body from the equal-and-opposite force on the central body
Relate the force readout in the orbital-mechanics simulation to M, m and r
misconceptions: Believing the gravitational force depends on the orbiting body's mass only, ignoring the central mass M
Treating the distance r as height above the surface rather than centre-to-centre separation
Believing a smaller orbiting mass experiences a smaller force for the same separation
Reading the force as increasing linearly with distance rather than with 1/r²
traps: Halving the distance quadruples the force (factor 4), not doubles it — the inverse-square term dominates
The force is symmetric: F on the orbiting body equals F on the central body, so mass_central has as much effect as mass_orbit
Force magnitude in newtons requires converting AU to metres (1 AU = 1.496 × 10¹¹ m) and solar masses to kilograms
Increasing mass_central from 1 to 4 M☉ multiplies the force by 4, not by the mass ratio squared
concepts.depth_test: Explain why reducing the initial distance between the two bodies from 2.0 AU to 1.0 AU quadruples the gravitational force, using F = G·M·m/r² and the inverse-square relation, rather than merely quoting the formula.

concepts.name: Circular, Elliptical, and Escape Trajectories
concepts.description: The shape of an orbit is set by the initial velocity magnitude and direction relative to the radial direction. A tangential velocity near the circular-orbit speed produces a circular orbit; a lower tangential component produces an elliptical orbit; a velocity at or above the escape velocity produces an open escape trajectory. Eccentricity e = 0 for a circle, 0 < e < 1 for an ellipse, and e ≥ 1 for escape.
core_skills: Predict the orbit shape (circular, elliptical, escape) from the initial velocity direction and magnitude
Use eccentricity to classify a trajectory: 0 = circular, 0–1 = elliptical, ≥1 = escape
Explain how a tangential (perpendicular) initial velocity is required for a circular orbit
Describe how increasing velocity at a fixed distance moves the orbit from circular to elliptical and ultimately to escape
Interpret the trajectory classification readout in the simulation
prerequisites: Velocity as a vector (magnitude and direction)
misconceptions: Believing a larger initial speed always gives a larger ellipse rather than possibly an escape trajectory
Believing the orbit is circular regardless of the initial velocity direction
Confusing eccentricity e = 1 (parabolic escape) with a highly elongated ellipse
Thinking escape velocity depends on the orbiting body's mass (it depends on the central field, not the orbiting mass)
traps: A radial (outward) initial velocity does not produce the same orbit as a tangential one — direction matters, not just speed
Escape occurs when speed ≥ escape velocity; beyond that the period and semi-major axis report infinite/∞
The velocity needed for a circular orbit is specific: too slow falls into an ellipse, too fast escapes
An escape trajectory still experiences gravitational force; it is open, not a closed ellipse
concepts.depth_test: In the simulation, predict and then verify which trajectory results from setting velocity magnitude 25 km/s at 90° (tangential) versus the same magnitude at 0° (radial), explaining the role of velocity direction using eccentricity.

concepts.name: Orbital Speed, Period, and Semi-Major Axis
concepts.description: For a stable orbit, the gravitational force provides the centripetal force, linking orbital speed, period, and semi-major axis. The period is the time for one complete orbit; the semi-major axis describes the average orbital size. The simulation reads out speed, period, eccentricity and semi-major axis so students can test the distance–period relationship.
core_skills: Relate orbital speed to the gravitational field strength at the orbit's location
Explain the distance–period relationship: orbits farther from the central body take longer to complete
Use the period readout (∞ for escape) to recognise open trajectories
Connect semi-major axis to the average size of the orbit and to the period
Analyse orbital speed along different parts of an elliptical orbit
prerequisites: Uniform circular motion and centripetal force
Mode-appropriate notions of period and distance
misconceptions: Believing all orbits around a given central body have the same period
Believing orbital speed is constant along an elliptical orbit
Confusing the semi-major axis with the instantaneous distance for a highly eccentric orbit
Believing a larger central mass always produces a longer period for the same distance (it produces a shorter one)
traps: Farther orbits are slower AND longer, so the period grows steeply with distance
A larger central mass (e.g., 4 M☉) at the same distance shortens the period, not lengthens it
The period readout shows ∞ for any escape trajectory — treat this as the open-orbit signal
Speed and period are not independent: changing either mass or distance changes both
concepts.depth_test: Set up an orbit and double the initial distance from the central body at the same tangential speed; predict whether the period increases or decreases and by roughly what factor, then verify with the simulation's period readout.

concepts.name: Escape Velocity and Binding to the Central Field
concepts.description: Escape velocity is the minimum speed an orbiting body needs at a given distance to leave the central body's gravitational field without further thrust. It depends only on the central mass and the distance, not on the orbiting body's mass. The simulation reports escape velocity at the current distance so students can compare it with their chosen initial speed.
core_skills: Define escape velocity as the minimum speed to leave the central field from a given distance
Explain that escape velocity is independent of the orbiting body's mass
Compare a chosen initial speed to the escape velocity to predict whether the orbit is bound or open
Relate escape velocity to the central mass and distance: higher central mass or smaller distance raises escape velocity
Use the escape-velocity readout to diagnose open versus closed trajectories
prerequisites: Energy: kinetic and gravitational potential energy
misconceptions: Believing a heavier orbiting body needs a higher escape speed
Believing escape velocity is reached only by leaving the gravitational 'reach' entirely rather than reaching an open trajectory
Treating escape velocity as a constant for the whole field rather than distance-dependent
Believing reaching exactly escape velocity gives a closed ellipse rather than a parabolic escape
traps: Escape velocity depends on the distance from the central body — it is lower farther out
If the chosen speed exceeds the reported escape velocity, the body escapes regardless of direction (as long as it is not directly into the surface)
At exactly escape speed the trajectory is open (parabolic), not a closed ellipse
Doubling the central mass multiplies the escape velocity by √2, not by 2
concepts.depth_test: At the default distance, compare the simulation's reported escape velocity with the default 25 km/s initial speed and predict whether the body escapes; explain your reasoning using the definition of escape velocity, then verify with the trajectory readout.

concepts.name: Kinetic and Gravitational Potential Energy in Orbits
concepts.description: The simulation tracks kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy of the orbiting body. Kinetic energy depends on speed; gravitational potential energy is negative and grows more negative (deeper) as the body moves closer to the central mass. In a bound orbit the total mechanical energy stays roughly constant while the two components trade off along the trajectory.
core_skills: Compute and compare kinetic energy (½mv²) of the orbiting body
Interpret gravitational potential energy as negative and decreasing (more negative) with lower altitude
Relate the kinetic and potential energy readouts to position along an elliptical orbit
Explain energy conservation in a bound orbit: the total stays approximately constant
Recognise that at escape the body has enough total energy for an open trajectory
prerequisites: Orbital Speed, Period, and Semi-Major Axis
misconceptions: Believing gravitational potential energy is positive and increases with altitude
Believing kinetic energy is constant around an elliptical orbit
Believing the total mechanical energy increases as the body falls inward
Confusing the exchange of kinetic and potential energy with a gain in total energy
traps: Potential energy is negative here; a deeper (more negative) value means closer to the central mass
At periapsis (closest approach) speed and kinetic energy peak while potential energy is most negative
The total mechanical energy stays approximately constant in a bound orbit — the simulation conserves energy via the symplectic integrator
For an escape trajectory, the kinetic energy exceeds the potential binding at the radius where it departs
concepts.depth_test: Watch the kinetic and potential energy readouts as the body travels around an elliptical orbit; state where each reaches its maximum and minimum and explain why the total stays roughly constant.
